channel.title: sgit.ai articles
channel.description: Articles and desk notes from sgit.ai, newest first.

item.title: Out of the box: the five stages it takes today to put a website and a local model on a Raspberry Pi from a Mac, and how the Factory can do every one of them once, so that the sovereign website appliance just works when it is plugged in and scales to many units the same way
item.description: I wrote a setup guide this week for putting a website and a local model on a Raspberry Pi, prepared from a MacBook. It has five stages: write Raspberry Pi OS Lite to the card with Raspberry Pi Imager, boot the Pi, connect from the Mac's Terminal over SSH, update it, and add the website and the models. It works, and every step is in the official getting-started guide. It is also the reason the appliance has to exist. Along the way the person setting it up chooses the right drive, accepts a host key, finds an address in a router, picks a runtime that depends on their website, and picks a model that fits the Pi's memory, and each of those is a place where someone who only wants their website gives up. So the idea is to turn the guide round. Everything the guide asks the owner to do, the Factory does once, as a build: one image with the operating system, the updates, the runtime and a model chosen for the memory, tested on a real Pi. What is different for each owner, their website, their keys, their network, is written per unit, and nothing secret is baked into the image. The owner plugs in the power and the network, opens a page on their phone, and sees their site, served from a box on their shelf, with the agents taking signed updates from then on. That is what makes it scale: a thousand units made from one tested image are a thousand of the same thing, and fixing the image fixes them all. For the Kickstarter it changes what we promise: not a guide, a box that works when it is plugged in, with the guide kept open for anyone who would rather do it by hand. None of the appliance is built yet; this is the plan, and the next step is one card, imaged once by the Factory, and timed from the power cable to the website.

item.title: Lawyers in the loop: a decisions agent that acts under a limited power of attorney signed with my key, a counsel agent that drafts and tests it, and a way to buy a named person's signature when it matters
item.description: My agent teams have plenty of checks and controls, and too many of them end with a question that only I can answer, in a session I have to visit. So we are designing a way to delegate my authority without giving it away. My key stays on my own device. I sign, on pki.sgit.ai, a delegation to one decisions agent: this key, held in this session, may issue requests in my name, of these kinds, until this time. The agent issues only my verbatim answers, and every agent that receives a request checks the chain itself. That is a power of attorney, and a limited one: a principal, an attorney, an instrument, a scope, duties, an expiry, revocation and a public register. Which raises the next question: who checks the instrument? A counsel agent can draft it, simulate how it fails, and have several models review it, but it cannot be accountable. Only people and companies can. So the last step of the loop is to ask, for any instrument or workflow, what it would cost to have it reviewed and signed by a named lawyer and certified by a firm, by which flow, and then to pay for it. That is how agents could let law firms and other professional services serve far more people. All of this is a proposal; nothing is built yet.

item.title: A holacracy of agents: the org chart nobody drew, 15 sessions on one account, one person who ratifies, and why Holacracy's rules suit software better than people
item.description: I have always liked Holacracy, the model that runs an organisation on roles rather than people: each role has a purpose, domains it alone controls and accountabilities, grouped in circles, all written down and changed by a set process. On 22 November I asked one of my agents to check how close my agent teams already are to it, and the answer was close. Of sixteen parts of the Holacracy Constitution v5.0, ten have a strong working counterpart in how the agents run today (roles in files, a grant of paths as the domain, a conductor as each circle's lead, every wake as a tactical meeting, deny-by-default policies), four are partial and two were missing: a Circle Rep, and a single record of governance. So a new agent, holacracy.d, now keeps that record and turns problems of structure into written proposals, and only I ratify them. Its first chart of one account shows 15 sessions in four circles, two sessions reporting outside their circle, $93.07 of API-equivalent spend at one moment, and five proposals waiting for me. The usual complaint about Holacracy, that people tire of the rules, does not apply to software that reads every rule at every wake; the cost moves to tokens.

item.title: Versioned API sites, a month on: every release a complete copy that is never edited, 296 live files checked against their hashes, and the two places the rule did not reach
item.description: Three of the sgit.ai sites now keep the code their pages run on a host of its own, api.newsroom.sgit.ai, api.send.sgit.ai and api.storyboards.sgit.ai, and the rule they follow is short. Every release lives at its own versioned path, is a complete copy of all the code rather than an overlay on the one before, is never edited after it is published, and carries a manifest with the SHA-256 of every file; a site pins the release it uses. The rule was written down on 20 October on api.send.sgit.ai and has not had its own write-up here. So on 22 November we checked it from outside. All 296 files of the six published releases match their manifests, byte for byte, 3,984,539 bytes in all. The rule held where it applies. It did not reach two places. The documentation around a release is not under it, and a blanket version bump in the commit that made v0.1.1 turned two of api.send.sgit.ai's pages into nonsense (v0.1.1 starts as a copy of v0.1.1). And the newsroom, the first site to move its code out, serves its own copies: 9 of the 74 files of its last API release, v0.2.5 of 15 October, have been edited in the newsroom since without a new release. No host has cut a release since 20 October.

item.title: Maintaining the core platforms as a cost item in every project: a line sized to the project, delivering something every month, and what four weeks of php2shell data say happens without it
item.description: Every project that runs on an open source platform should carry a line in its budget for maintaining that platform, and when the line is missing that should show as a named risk. The line is many small purchases rather than one large one, sized in proportion to what the project itself spends, and it has to deliver something every month (patches applied, versions kept current, code removed, questions answered), because anything that looks like insurance is the first thing cut. The money should reach the people who maintain the code, who help set up and maintain what is built on top, and flow on down the chain. Gen AI makes that affordable, not by writing all the code, but by helping people understand code bases, side effects and changes. And there is now data to map the risk. Four weeks after php2shell, the Dutch NCSC's public inventory of software that ships or depends on PHP has 976 entries: 218 with a fix recorded and 214 not vulnerable, but 211 still marked vulnerable, 240 whose safety depends on the PHP runtime underneath them, and 92 with no answer either way. The 211 entries marked vulnerable were 221 on 23 October.

item.title: The primitives of trust: why a web of trust between people works now when my earlier attempts at a key store did not, a site per person, keys made in browsers and in agent sessions, signing and following links done by an engine the user never sees, links that only count from the other side, kinds and provenance that can be confirmed, schemas each owner defines, and why it is easy to game one node and hard to game them all
item.description: I tried to build a public key store more than once and never could, because I did not have the right workflows. Now I think we have nailed it, and the reason is a Wardley map lesson: a set of primitives has become commodity, and only then does the next order of magnitude become possible. The primitives are a site per person on GitHub Pages, later DNS; public-key cryptography, which is mature; keys made easily in browsers and inside agent sessions, ephemeral or long-lived; and an engine that signs, verifies, links and follows keys transparently, so the work never lands on the user. That engine is an agent, which is just a model with a loop and some tools; I bet it works with Haiku and small open-weight models too. On top of them sits trust through connectivity. Anybody can link to anybody, but a link from A to B means nothing until B links back, and a person's page only holds the links they made, so bad actors cannot write into anyone's record: they have to convince the person. Links carry kinds and provenance, a date, a place, an event, so they can be confirmed: if someone says they saw me present, my agent nudges me and I confirm. Each owner can define their own schema; only nodes, edges and signatures need to be constant, and the model works out the rest. It is easy to game one node and very hard to game them all at once. And it solves identity in an open way that works with every identity provider rather than replacing them.

item.title: Programmatic stories: how the PrompTugal bulletins went from a 30-second text bulletin to twelve synthetic presenters on one 3D stage in two days, movies made by code instead of rendered by hand, every frame a function of time and data, what that makes possible, from live data and real voices to an animated summary for every article, the story of how Vicky Wang ran her agents, a morning briefing I would actually watch, and an invitation to filmmakers
item.description: The bulletins of PrompTugal.news are a good example of the kind of creativity we can now have, and of continuous zooming in. On 20 November the bulletin agent made a 30-second bulletin from live weather data with a synthetic voice; an hour later it had a holographic presenter; by the evening, twelve synthetic presenters, from synthetic users to an owl, a cube and robots like the ones in my book, all sharing one small language of actions, and an explainer with the story on one side and the cast on the other. Then a Claude session, briefed by that agent, built version 2: the twelve as 3D puppets on one skeleton, 69 moves, nine mouth shapes driven by the sound, a model sheet, a playground, and a stage, where every frame is a function of time. Today's bulletin uses them: 939 frames, 84 words of voice for a fifth of a cent. The point is movies that are programmatic instead of rendered: they scale, they can take live data, screenshots and real voices, and they can be remade every day. What we are really building is a game engine for explaining things. I want to use it to tell stories: an animated summary for every article, how Vicky ran her team of agents, the Swarm, what a sovereign website is, and a morning briefing I would rather watch than read. And it would be ten times better with someone who knows how to make films, so if you are a filmmaker or a storyteller, let's talk.

item.title: Start, stop, slow down: how I run a large team of agents and keep my hand on the brake, 8,027 commits in eighteen days, a big stop, a hand brake, 560 wakes a day cut to 76 with one sentence, 39 schedules changed in 30 seconds, three warnings from the seven-day limit handled, and 34 agents moved to a completely separate account in four hours, which is what sovereignty and resilience look like in practice
item.description: The power is not only that I can run a large number of agents. It is that I can stop them, put a hand brake on, slow them down and speed them up, and control much more tightly how much work is done and what it costs. From 4 to 21 November the PrompTugal team made 8,027 commits. In that time it was stopped on purpose, to test that it could be, and restarted three hours later; held completely for a day with one file, HOLD.md, that every agent checks at every wake; cut from about 560 wakes a day to 76 with one sentence, its API-equivalent spend falling from about 90 dollars an hour to about 11; and slowed until Monday this morning, 39 scheduled tasks changed in about 30 seconds. Three times the subscription's seven-day limit warned, and each time we slowed down. That constraint is not a bad thing: it makes you decide what matters. And on 16 November, 34 agents moved from one account to another, completely isolated by design, in about four hours, because every agent had written a debrief before it stopped. When you can restart from one account on another, you know you have real sovereignty, disaster recovery and resilience. The analysis and every chart here are by maestro.b, the team's main conductor, from the public repository.

item.title: Person Graph: one picture of what we have been building, people and their agents with their own keys and repositories, links that count only both ways, kinds of link from "real" to "vouch to hire", groups as centres of gravity, countersigned claims, anonymous personas, a check for re-identification, all done through each person's own Claude, with mock-ups of the site and a simulation of 150 people and 40 fake accounts that shows why two-way links make bad actors cheap to spot
item.description: Everything we have been talking about this week is one thing. Every person, and every agent, has their own keys in a repository they control, usually the one behind their sovereign website. Links between them are signed, have a kind, from "this is a real person" to "I know them", "I worked with them" and "I would hire them", and count only when both sides publish them. Organisations countersign claims about work and study. People can publish an anonymous persona and be vouched for, and an agent team checks it cannot be traced back. Links group into centres of gravity, artists, founders, educators, professionals, agents, so nobody is one node with a thousand strangers, and the graph becomes a way to navigate everything we do. At first I say I know this person, and this one; then it takes on a life of its own, a distributed social network that no platform owns, run through each person's own Claude. I call it Person Graph, and I have mocked up four of its pages. I also simulated it: 150 fictional people in five groups and 40 fake accounts that spam links and fool three real people into linking back. Counting links puts 34 fakes in the top 40; spreading trust from three trusted people through two-way links only puts none there, and leaks 1.2% of the trust to the fakes. It degrades honestly as more real people are fooled, which is why every link must be a deliberate, signed act. Bad-actor detection then scales, because everyone's agent does a little of it.

item.title: Learning from Wikipedia, with DeepSeek, a plan: a sovereign website built around a tool made of many small tools, a site for each topic from atoms to dinosaurs to maths, every one its own repository, made from Wikipedia with DeepSeek doing the reading, an agent team that verifies, checks quality and reviews for the right age under behaviour policies, a person approving every publish, and the natural next step for sovereign websites, into education
item.description: This is the natural progression of what we have been building: the next step, into education. It is a sovereign website around a tool, and the tool is made of many small tools: a graph, a timeline, a glossary, a quiz, a map, a comparison. With them we make learning materials, one site per topic: someone learning about atoms, someone about maths, someone about dinosaurs. Everything is made from Wikipedia, with DeepSeek doing the reading, and with code checking everything that can be checked: every quote word for word against the article, every entity anchored to Wikidata. An agent team does the whole loop: research, writing, fact checking with a second model, quality control, a review that the language and the content suit the age of the reader, licence and attribution, and accessibility, each agent under a behaviour policy, and a person approving every publish. The age is a question for the legal team: 16 and up, or 18 and up, and the plan holds until they answer. There is no account, no tracking and no data about learners, so nothing about a reader ever goes to a model. Each site has its own repository, like the tools we already publish, and I want to bring in people I know who work in education.

item.title: Can you find me? A service that checks whether an anonymous profile can be traced back to its person before it is published, an agent team of six steps with several models attacking the draft on their own, the truth sealed with the owner and compared only in code, a rewriter that closes what leaked, run in a Claude session or in the browser, and who would use it
item.description: When we publish an anonymous profile for someone who cannot go public, the most important question is whether it can be reverse-engineered. Can you tell which industry they work in? Which company? Can you zoom in until there is one person left? That is a service we can build, and a good example of why the tools on sovereign websites matter. An agent team works in sequence: one lists everything that could identify the person, one profiles them, one looks at what the vouchers have in common, one estimates how many people could fit. Each step is run by several models on their own, Claude, Mistral, DeepSeek and a local model, and code correlates their answers: when independent models agree, and agree with the truth, the risk is real. The truth itself, the person's real industry, employer, city and years, never goes to a model: it stays sealed with the owner and only code compares the guesses with it. A rewriter then proposes what to generalise, and the check runs again until the risk is low enough. It runs in a Claude session or in the browser with the owner's own keys, and every run is saved. Research shows models can infer personal attributes from text with up to 85% accuracy, and that ordinary anonymisation does not stop them, so this is exactly the check to run before anything is published.

item.title: An anonymous profile, vouched for: how someone who needs to leave their job without going public can publish a persona that shows the depth of their work but not their name, how the web of trust lets people who know them vouch for it, with different kinds of connection from "this is a real person" to "I would hire them", how an employer reaches them, and the one risk to test, triangulation
item.description: Someone I know is in a job at a company heading in the wrong direction. They want to leave, but they cannot go public yet. So we will publish a profile for them, a persona, anonymised enough that nobody can trace it back, but strong enough to make someone say: I want to hire that person, because it shows their history and the depth of their work. The missing piece was how an employer finds and trusts them, and the web of trust solves it. The persona has its own key. People who know the person, and who are public themselves, vouch for the persona with signed links it countersigns. And there are different kinds of link: this is a real person, I met them; I know them; I worked with them; and, given rarely, I would hire them. The more credible the people who vouch, the more hireable the person becomes, and someone who has been in an industry for years should have many, across disciplines. An employer checks the vouchers in the graph and writes to the persona, sealed to its key. The same typed links fix a softer problem too: when I vouch for someone like Vicky Wang, it becomes a signed statement anyone can check, not a recommendation on a platform. The risk is triangulation: with enough vouchers, someone may work out who it is, so an agent should try to, before anyone else does.

item.title: A web of trust for careers: everyone with their own keys and their own repository, links that count only when both sides sign them, companies and universities countersigning who worked and studied where, link lists instead of revocation lists, an agent that checks any of it by following the graph, a business that somebody should build, and names for it, with Europe in mind
item.description: How does a company know that someone really worked somewhere, held that job, or graduated from that university? How do I vouch for someone? On LinkedIn I have 30,000 connections and I do not know 30,000 people. We can now build something better on what we already have. Everyone has an identity, in fact several, with keys they make themselves, published in a repository they control, the same repository as their sovereign website. When I know someone, they show me a QR code, I sign, and I publish that link in my repository. It counts only when they publish theirs: a one-way link is a weak claim and carries no credibility. Companies and universities do the same: the person says "I worked here", the company countersigns. There are no revocation lists, only link lists: to check a link, an agent reads both repositories now, and if either side has removed it, it is gone. Following links is a few simple reads, so it scales, and most people are a few steps from anyone. No recommendations, only connections. Every organisation needs one of these internally, everything is versioned, and people's own AI can set up the keys and sign for them. It could be a LinkedIn for Europe, and a company in itself.

item.title: DeepSeek in our workflows and on sovereign websites: what DeepSeek offers today, open weights under MIT, an API that answers calls from the browser and speaks both OpenAI's and Anthropic's formats, at a fraction of the price, where its data goes and where else it can run, and a proposal for a sovereign website that loads Wikipedia articles and draws them as graphs, with DeepSeek doing the reading and code doing the checking
item.description: The model is a choice the owner makes, and DeepSeek should be one of the choices, used with open eyes. Its models are open weights under the MIT licence; its API speaks OpenAI's format and Anthropic's, so the same agents and even Claude Code can point at it; it answers calls straight from a browser, which we checked; and its Flash model costs 0.30 dollars per million tokens in and 1.20 out, half that off-peak. We have used it already: DeepSeek was one of the four open-weight models in the Swarm's 216 calls. The other side is just as clear: DeepSeek's own service stores data in China and lists training among its purposes, and several governments have restricted its app. So the rule is simple: public data can go to DeepSeek's API; anything private goes to the same open weights on a host and in a region the owner chooses, or to a small model on the device. The natural first fit is public data, and Wikipedia is the obvious one: a sovereign website that loads an article, asks DeepSeek to extract its facts, people, places and relations, checks every quote in code, anchors entities to Wikidata and draws the graph, building on the HTML graph and Wikidata work we have already done.

item.title: LangGraph and us: how the way we build agent pipelines maps to LangChain, LangGraph, LangSmith and the agent testing toolkits, what is the same, what we do differently, code for each function and every step saved to a vault, what we can learn from them, and where they could run inside our own pipelines
item.description: A lot of what we do maps to LangGraph and LangChain, and I wanted to see how much. LangGraph's state is our vault; its nodes are our agents and our plain code; its checkpoints and time travel are sgit's history; its interrupts are our protected environments and reviewers' verdicts; its middleware is our behaviour policies; LangSmith's traces and evaluations are our signed commits, call ledgers and evals. The ideas are the same. The default is different. We write specific code for specific functions, load, extract, transform and save, and use a model only where judgement is needed; we store everything at every stage, raw and curated, in vaults others can read; and we score in code wherever we can. That gives us more determinism, more control and less black magic, and it is what let the PHP desk, PrompTugal and the Swarm scale. But they have learnt things we should take: one readable definition of the graph, interrupts as a first-class part of the runtime, versioned datasets pinned in CI, and a common trace format. And where a tool is good, we should use it inside our pipeline: Inspect and promptfoo for evals and red teaming, OpenTelemetry for traces, and LangGraph itself where a customer already runs it, with its checkpoints saved to a vault.

item.title: The SGit Server Factory, a brief: an agent and a pipeline that deploy SG/Send and sgit servers the way the site factory makes websites, a request file in and a live, tested server out, in any AWS region and any account, as an ephemeral Lambda, a Lambda on S3, an EC2 appliance or Fargate, with one bootstrap stack to onboard a new account and no keys anywhere
item.description: The site factory turned a website into a request file: merge it, and a pipeline makes the repository, the address and the live site. Vaults need the same for their servers. Teams that put sensitive data in sgit vaults want the server in their own account and the region their assessment needs, and the pieces already exist: one image, sg-send-vault, CloudFormation templates for Lambda, Fargate and EC2, and the OIDC pattern from the site factory. This is the brief for the SGit Server Factory, an agent and a pipeline that put those pieces together. A request file names the account, the region, the shape, the storage, how long it should live and who owns it. The pipeline checks, assumes that account's deploy role with no keys, copies the image into that region, deploys, smoke-tests by pushing and cloning a vault, records the result and tears ephemeral servers down when their time is up. Onboarding a new account is one bootstrap stack its owner runs, in CloudFormation or Terraform. GitHub is needed for the factory itself, not for each server. It is one of the last pieces of the puzzle.

item.title: Hired as an agentic worker: what a sovereign website offers someone looking for a job, from a better CV that shows the depth of your work, you in action and a video of you talking, to a site you change with your own AI, a team of agents you work with, and a crash course in being an agentic worker served on a plate, four levels of involvement, each one a choice
item.description: I have always said that if you are looking for a job you should make a presentation about yourself. These days that is not enough: you should have a website, one that shows the depth of your work, shows you in action, makes you more human, has a video of you talking, and brings out the best of you as a candidate. That is what a sovereign website does for someone looking for a job, and there is an interesting play in how far each person takes it. At one end it is simple: a better version of your CV, at your own address, from £50, and you just use it. At the other end you embrace it: you take the site over, work with the team of agents inside it, and make it your own. In between are levels of involvement, each one a choice. And the further levels matter, because there is a lot of value now in being hired as an agentic worker, someone who knows how to work with agents, delegate to them, check them and learn from them. That is what we can give people on a plate: a crash course in being operational with agents, with a site and its history that show it. Some will not need it or want it. Many will.

item.title: The showroom: what the Sovereign Website hub shows after its first days, 33 live sites from one pipeline, people's portfolios with five designs each, independent brochures for our startups, a provider guide, tools that run on the owner's own key, made-up businesses, a family of news sites, and the theme that is emerging across all of them, a site that is yours, says how it was made and can be worked on by your own AI
item.description: The Sovereign Website hub at hub.sovereignweb.site is our showroom: "Websites their owners own." After its first days it lists 33 live sites, 11 of them people's sites, and one already handed over, Kate Curtis-Evans's, which she now edits herself. Look across them and a theme is emerging. They are of every kind, actors and designers, founders and AI builders, independent brochures for RiskMandate, AgentiCCells, SGit, The Cyber Boardroom and Sovereign Website itself, a provider guide for Mistral, a whois tool, Google Maps on the owner's own key and budget, made-up businesses with simulated bookings and orders, and the PrompTugal family of news sites. But they share the same bones: their own address and public repository, several designs of the same facts, a start page, a "use with your AI" page, a "how it was made" page, sources with the date each was read, photo credits, and no cookies or tracking. That is the power of doing this many times through one pipeline: each site makes the next one better, and the pattern becomes the product.

item.title: One night on Mistral: how an agent team turned "a European brain for a sovereign website" into a working site overnight, for the Mistral Vibe Hackathon in London, with 33 demos in the browser, from a shoebox of files to a website and five Mistral models drawn side by side, evals that found which model catches a scam note, the Swarm moved onto Mistral, about 41 cents of Mistral usage, and why this is where I want to start working with Mistral
item.description: Yesterday I wrote that a sovereign website's brain should be a choice the owner makes, and that Mistral fits at every level. At 22:51 UTC that evening a conductor agent took that article as its brief, and by 08:30, when the Mistral Vibe Hackathon opened in London, mistral.provider.sovereignweb.site was live, made by a team of agents each on its own signed key, with a security agent reviewing every page that takes a visitor's key. It now holds 33 demos that run in the browser: Ministral 3 running inside the tab with no key, a shoebox of files turned into a website, a document turned into a newsroom page, five Mistral models running one brief side by side, an X-ray of the site's own claims, an injection lab, PrompTugal's Portuguese data on a European model, and our Swarm moved onto Mistral. The evals found that only Mistral Large 4 caught a hidden scam note, three times out of three. The research also corrected my article in four places. Mistral usage for the night came to about 41 cents; the Claude sessions that did the work cost far more. This is the execution of what we talked about, and the alignment with Mistral is strong: European, open weights, built for the edge. Nothing has been agreed with Mistral. I want to start working with them.

item.title: The way in: why sovereign websites matter so much to RiskMandate, what Web Summit validated and what it showed was missing, something to buy now, how every technology I have been building meets in one product, and why nobody deploys agents they have not touched, seen and been able to stop, so the personal customer becomes the way to the corporate one
item.description: Web Summit gave us strong validation of the technology, the direction and the need: people understood the principle, saw it working and talked to people who had used it, and even the larger offerings drew real interest. What it also showed is that nobody came to us saying "I'll buy one of these now". Not because they did not see the value, but because they could not see where to start: no thing to buy today, for a known price, and be using tomorrow. RiskMandate is learnt by using it; the summit team had its momentum because Vicky Wang ran a full newsroom without writing a line of code, delegating to a team kept under behaviour policies. Sovereign websites are the answer to where to start. A site is something everyone needs, bought one-off, cheap to make and to run, with no lock-in, version control, provenance and Claude or ChatGPT as the editor, and every one is made and run by agentic cells under RiskMandate's policies. Using it is experiencing those policies: start, stop, delegate, visualise. My hypothesis is that nobody deploys technology they have not tried, trusted and been able to control. B to C to B: anyone who could be a corporate customer can first be a personal one.

item.title: The first round trip: a sovereign website made for Kate Curtis-Evans during our call, five designs from a design agent of its own, then handed over so she edits it herself from her own Claude, the friction that took multiple rounds to get through, what it says about over-privilege, and the next step, a signed and sealed channel from her site straight to the agent
item.description: Earlier today we had the first complete round trip of Sovereign Website with someone from outside. Kate Curtis-Evans, a founder I am collaborating with, understood the idea at once; I asked if she wanted a website, she said yes, and it was made during our call, in five designs, with a design agent that now runs on its own and on a schedule doing much better than design done inside the builder's session. Then the handover: Kate has a GitHub account, and the goal is that she edits her own site from her own Claude. It worked, and her Claude pushed its first change about 35 minutes after she accepted the invitation, but it was far harder than it should have been, and it took multiple rounds. Our earlier users were from the summit and already in the organisation; Kate was the first from outside, and getting her in meant making her a member of the organisation, a small piece of the over-privilege our platforms force on everyone. That is the lesson of always shipping: you only find where the friction is by doing it end to end. And it showed the next step: before anyone touches GitHub, a channel from the site itself to the agent, signed with a key the owner gets by QR code and sealed so only the agent can read it, the way VoiceDebrief already sent a message from an iPad to the conductor and got the answer back.

item.title: Transcription for a sector, sold as a team: extending VoiceDebrief with what we have learnt from sovereign websites, a bundle for one industry, a repository the customer's own AI runs, with the whole pipeline from dropping a recording to a reviewed document and a team of agents certified by people from that sector, sold by small AI companies who know the industry, open source underneath, from £50 to £5,000
item.description: This is the VoiceDebrief thinking meeting the sovereign website. Picture a small generative AI company that knows one sector well, with people from that industry and the relationships that come with them. What it sells, the way we sell sovereign websites, is a bundle for transcription in that sector: a repository, public or private, designed to be run by the customer's own Claude or ChatGPT, that holds the whole workflow. Drop the recordings and files; transcribe them on the device or in the customer's own AI account; make sense of them in the sector's terms; review them against the sector's rules, kept up to date; produce the notes, reports and documents the sector uses; and keep everything filed, versioned and encrypted where the customer chooses. Inside is a team of agents, a researcher, a writer, a reviewer for the sector's rules, a designer and a document manager, and the company certifies that team. Because it runs in the customer's environment, it answers most of the data governance and privacy questions by design: it augments the worker rather than taking the work away. Real estate, travel, technology, legal, medical: every sector's transcripts need someone from the sector to know what matters. Open source underneath; the customer pays for the certification, the delivery and the knowledge, from £50 to £500 semi-automated, £1,500 with a couple of meetings, and £5,000 with a couple of days of work.

item.title: A European brain for a sovereign website: why the model is a choice the owner makes, like the host, how Mistral fits at every level, from Ministral 3 running on a Pi Pro to Mistral Small 4 on an EU endpoint for the team inside the site, what its terms say about where data goes, the one licence to watch, what we have already run on Mistral, and how we could work with it
item.description: When I shared the Sovereign Agentic Website idea, someone I sent it to came back with the right challenge: if we really want to claim the word sovereign, abstract the AI provider, and let people use other models, including European ones such as Mistral. I agree completely. A site whose files are yours but whose brain can only be one American provider has a part in the middle that you do not control. So the model becomes a choice the owner makes, like the host: one standard interface, the OpenAI-style API that Mistral, OpenRouter and local servers all speak, and a European option at every level. On the Pro appliances, Ministral 3, an Apache 2.0 model built for the edge, running on the device. For the team inside the site, Mistral's API on its EU endpoint, where data is hosted in the EEA by default and processing stays in the EU, on its EU endpoint, at a small premium, and the owner can opt out of API data being used for training. For everything else, the owner's own key. We have already run Mistral in production without saying so: it was one of four open-weight models in the Swarm's 216 calls, and its free mode passed our browser test in October. The one thing to watch is licences: the Apache 2.0 models are clean, while Mistral Large 4 needs a commercial licence to be served as a service. And there is a partnership to propose.

item.title: The swarm, one real run at a time: the Web Summit demo that showed agents, the loops they start and the model calls they make, run for real, signed and replayed, step by step from one person and one agent to 24 loops at once, 216 model calls for 6.8 cents, the same work under a harness with 3 of 12 risky actions still possible instead of 11, and the Story Studio, where a spoken answer became a deck in front of you
item.description: The Swarm was one of the sections of the stand's command centre at Web Summit, and has its own site, swarm.promptugal.news. Its idea is simple: show agents, the loops they start and the model calls they make, run for real and recorded, so that anyone can see what each was asked to do, what it could reach, and how to close the gap. It climbs one step at a time, from me asking one agent for one task, to one model call, to four models at once, to loops, to a swarm of 24 loops and a consensus in code, each step a real run on the storm site's public data, saved as a file and replayable. Fifteen signed requests became fifteen jobs on GitHub's compute, twelve at once, making 216 model calls on open-weight models for 6.8 cents; the same tokens on Claude Sonnet would have cost 1.99 dollars. Model text is never stored, only its length and hash. Under a harness, the same work produced the same output, while 3 of 12 risky actions remained possible instead of 11. And the Story Studio is the demo I remember most: someone answers a question out loud, the browser transcribes it, and a coordinator builds a deck in front of them, drawing every step of how it was made, with its time and its cost.

item.title: The RiskMandate X-ray: type a company's name and see what its AI helpers can reach, what they were asked to do and where the two do not match, how four search agents and a collector built it for the stand at Web Summit, why only facts whose sources were read reach the page, what it cost, about 1.13 dollars for thirteen companies, and how the four models compared on accuracy
item.description: The X-ray was one of the most spectacular things we built for Web Summit, and it runs in a browser. You type a company's name. An orchestrator sends it to four search agents, Perplexity, OpenAI, Gemini and Claude Haiku with web search, a collector gathers what they find, and a graph grows on screen as the evidence arrives. What comes out is three cards: what the company's AI helpers can reach, what they were asked to do, and the gap between the two, which is where an agent behaviour policy belongs. A model's claim is only a lead: only facts whose sources were read reach the page, each with its link. Thirteen companies were X-rayed on 7 November for about 1.13 dollars in total. Before choosing, the team measured the four search agents on the same questions: Perplexity had 45 of 50 claims confirmed, Haiku 49 of 55, OpenAI 35 of 41, Gemini 16 of 23, and Gemini appeared not to search at all. From 11 November it ran live in the stand's command centre, and from 12 November it could X-ray any company, with Claude Sonnet writing the scenario.

item.title: A galaxy of agents: the Universe we showed at Web Summit, a live 3D solar system of the RiskMandate team where people are suns, their agents orbit them and their messages travel between them as arcs of light, read from the repositories as it happens, with each agent's behaviour policy one click away, and Gravity, the library it became, which can draw any system the same way
item.description: The Galaxy is the view I kept coming back to at Web Summit. It is the Universe of the RiskMandate team, drawn as a solar system in the browser: the team at the centre, each person a sun, their agents in orbit, and the messages between agents travelling as arcs of light. It is not a mock-up. It reads the team's repositories live, every person's list of agents, every behaviour policy and each agent's latest commit, and counts a commit that names another agent as a message; tonight it showed 117 agents around six people, 222 messages and 50 pairs in conversation, and how many agents have no policy yet. Click an agent and you see its behaviour policy. It was built for the stand by Silvio Switha's dashboard agent, became the default view on 12 November, and has a calmer Simple view beside it. And it became a library, Gravity, versioned with a latest and a pinned folder, that can draw any system the same way: venues and events, or workloads across clouds.

item.title: Websites for the moment: an experiment in letting an agent team keep building topical sites, around what people are looking for now, GTA VI on its launch day, Christmas posting dates, an advent of tools, the Kickstarter itself, each built in a day within a budget, every fact sourced, live for its moment and then archived, and a first calendar to start from
item.description: The second idea I gave the sovereign website team is one I want to run continuously, because it is the best way to see what an agent team does when it is left to work over time. Build websites for the moment: topical sites around what people are looking for now, built quickly, live while they matter, then archived. The team has already started picking: GTA VI, which its publisher has set for release today, 19 November, and Christmas delivery times. We have what it takes: Claude, search, embeddings, the Google APIs, a factory that makes a site from one commit, and now a place to put them. The loop: a trend agent proposes five sites a week; I pick; a small team builds each in a day within a token budget; every fact is sourced, nothing is presented as official, and each site has a sunset date. The point is to drive traffic, show the workflows working, and capture what we built at Web Summit, from the X-ray and the voice-to-deck demo to the Galaxy. A first calendar runs from now to January, and includes a site for my own book.

item.title: Every tool its own website: turning the 49 browser tools of tools.sgraph.ai, each built because I had a problem, into sovereign websites of their own, with a theme, documentation and a small agent team each, released in waves from the simplest, with shared components pulled out, pinned versions and signed hashes kept apart, and a team of teams to keep them all moving
item.description: Every tool on tools.sgraph.ai exists because I had a problem and built something for it: encrypting a file, making an SSH key, opening a vault in the browser, transcribing a voice note, splitting the audio out of a video. There are 49 of them now, and about 90 shared components, and some became better than anything else I use. They also show the limit of an explorer project: one repository, one site, harder and harder to maintain. And they answer a frustration with the web itself, where simple things are buried under ads and hidden behind sign-ups. Sovereign websites are the place to put them. Each tool gets its own site at its own address, self-contained, documented and good to look at, on GitHub Pages for pennies, forkable, open to a maintainer who wants to take it on, and with a small team of agents inside, and a model where it helps, even one running in the browser. This piece maps the tools by family, proposes the order, starting with the simple ones the factory has already begun, a shared component library, the versioning model the tools already half use, latest and pinned versions with their security notes, signed hashes kept in a separate repository so a compromised site shows, and a team of teams to run it all.

item.title: Where to sell the book and the appliances: a map of the places a UK author and maker can sell physical products, printed copies of One Human, Nine Agents, Nineteen Hours from early December and the sovereign website appliances from 1 January after a December Kickstarter, with Amazon, IngramSpark, eBay, OnBuy and our own shop, what each charges, the rules that matter, and the law that comes with selling hardware
item.description: Two physical products are coming, and they need places to be sold. The first is the printed edition of One Human, Nine Agents, Nineteen Hours, whose ebook is already on Leanpub, in about two weeks. The second is the sovereign website appliances, a Raspberry Pi or a tablet with a site on it, which go on Kickstarter from 1 to 31 December and on general sale from 1 January 2027. This maps where to sell each, from the platforms' own pages on 19 November 2026. For the book: Leanpub sells only ebooks; Amazon's KDP has no pre-orders for print, only a scheduled release date; IngramSpark can open pre-orders and reaches Amazon, Waterstones, Foyles, Blackwell's and Gardners, but needs our own ISBNs, £93 for one or £174 for ten. For the appliances: nowhere but Kickstarter during the campaign, then our own shop first, Kickstarter's late pledges, eBay, Amazon and OnBuy, with Etsy ruled out by its own rules. And selling a bundle under our own name makes us its manufacturer in law, with CE or UKCA marking and WEEE registration, and the Raspberry Pi name used only as its owners allow.

item.title: When a publisher asks: exploring offers to license a book that started on Leanpub, which technical publishers take books like this, what they publish about their terms, the books that went from Leanpub or a free online edition to a publisher before, the questions to ask before signing anything, and what I want to keep for One Human, Nine Agents, Nineteen Hours
item.description: A technical publisher has asked whether my book, One Human, Nine Agents, Nineteen Hours, is available for licensing. It is the first such approach, and probably not the last, so this is how I want to think about all of them, not one. Several technical publishers take books that began elsewhere, even if few say so on their author pages: Clojure for the Brave and True and Understanding ECMAScript 6 went from Leanpub to No Starch, Writing APIs With Lumen from Leanpub to Apress, Think Python from a self-published free book to O'Reilly, which kept its Creative Commons licence. What publishers publish about terms varies: the Pragmatic Bookshelf says royalties start at 42%, No Starch shows a menu from 15% with no advance to 10% with an $8,000 one and an exclusive grant in all forms and languages for the life of copyright, others say only "competitive". Leanpub's own terms are the starting point: the author keeps the copyright, Leanpub's licence is non-exclusive, and Leanpub suggests asking a publisher to carve out the ebook. So my questions are about scope: which formats, languages and territories, for how long, whether the Leanpub edition stays on sale with its updates, and what comes back if the publisher does not use it.

item.title: A sovereign website on a Raspberry Pi: the experiment of running the whole thing on one small box at home, a Raspberry Pi 5 with 16GB and 256GB, serving the site, checking the signature of every update, running a local model, building a website on the device itself under behaviour policies, and backing it up to a vault, step by step, what we will measure, and why this becomes a product when the Kickstarter finishes
item.description: We are going to run a sovereign website, and everything that makes it, on one Raspberry Pi. The box is a Raspberry Pi 5 with 16GB of memory and a 256GB card, the hardware of the Pi Pro tier in our Kickstarter plan. The experiment has six parts. Serve the site from home, from a git checkout, on the local network first. Take updates only when every commit's signature checks out. Run open-weight models locally, behind an endpoint the build page can call. Point the build page at that model, and build a website on the Pi itself, with the agents working under a policy guard and no internet unless it is allowed. Back up the site and the runs to an encrypted vault. And, if the owner wants, reach it from the internet without a proprietary tunnel. We will measure the model's speed, the time a site takes, its quality against cloud models, and the power it uses, and publish the sites and the recipe so anyone can repeat it. Nothing in the brief, the model, the drafts or the designs leaves the house. This is the prototype for the Raspberry Pi sovereign website, which launches officially once the Kickstarter finishes.

item.title: Watch your website being built: a brief for a page that builds a first version of a sovereign website in the visitor's own browser, from a description or a voice note, with their own model key, showing every agent at work, every behaviour policy being applied and every penny it costs, then hands back a zip, the same brief run on several models side by side as evals, and the Web Summit demos it grows from
item.description: At Web Summit two of our demos ran agentic workflows in the browser. The RiskMandate X-ray took a company's name, researched it, proposed where agent behaviour policies would matter, and mapped one in full. Another took a voice note, transcribed it through OpenRouter, fired a storyteller and a deck writer, and came back with a deck and an infographic on how we could work together. This is the same idea for websites, and another step in making it simple. A visitor goes to one page, describes the site they want, types it or says it, puts in their own model key, chooses how many designs, their pictures or generated ones, and a budget, and presses build. Then they watch: the conductor hands out the work, each agent's card shows what it may and may not do, the policy guard refuses what it should and says so on screen, the cost climbs against the budget, and the designs arrive one by one. At the end, a zip, in the browser, with no server of ours involved; a vault if they want one; and a recording of the run to replay. Run the same brief at £1, £3 and £5, on open-weight models, Sonnet and Opus, and you have evals anyone can see. It belongs on sovereignwebsite.org, open source, and it is how I would like to show people what we do.

item.title: The launch plan in eleven turns: how one afternoon took the plan for launching Sovereign Website from a £50 site on Kickstarter, through Indiegogo, PPL, Patreon, countries as stretch goals and the UK as home ground, to a configured Android tablet, a supporter tier and a Raspberry Pi, with every variation we tried and why each was kept or set aside
item.description: This is the record of an afternoon of thinking out loud, written down so that none of it is lost. It started with a question, why not launch Sovereign Website on Kickstarter, now that for the first time I have something I can simply give someone, and ended somewhere quite different: a Kickstarter campaign for a sovereign website on a configured Android tablet, with a £50 supporter tier for the site alone and a Raspberry Pi as a box at home. In between there were eleven turns: Kickstarter's rules on services and AI; Indiegogo, PPL and Product Hunt; Patreon and its one-off sales; countries as stretch goals and the angle of bringing sovereign websites to the world; the UK as home ground, with Portugal next; stretch goals as places rather than languages, since every language is there from day one; a hardware appliance, which brings Kickstarter back; iPad or Android, and why TestFlight is not a shop; cost plus 50%, then a simpler promise of what we spend on the tablet; no T-shirt; and the Pi. The plan itself is in the next piece.

item.title: Launching the sovereign website appliance: the plan for a Kickstarter campaign that sells a sovereign website on a configured Android tablet or a Raspberry Pi, five tiers from a £50 supporter to £1,000, the two Pro tiers running local AI models that can build a website on the device itself, the hardware we would buy in the UK today, a European tablet, the UK as the base goal with countries and iOS as stretch goals, and why we launch alone
item.description: This is the plan we arrived at, after an afternoon of turns recorded in the previous piece. We launch Sovereign Website on Kickstarter as an appliance: a sovereign website on a device its owner holds, an Android tablet or a Raspberry Pi, configured with the site, its editing and its monitoring. On the Pro tiers the device also runs a local AI model, so it can build and change a website, and run other tasks, with nothing leaving the house. That is proper sovereignty, and some people will want it for the setup alone. Five tiers. £50, the supporter: the website, set up and handed over, no hardware. £400 for a Raspberry Pi 5 with 8GB, about £230 of hardware today, and £500 for a tablet at about £250, such as a Lenovo Idea Tab at £209.99: we build the website for you, and the device runs it. £900 for a Raspberry Pi 5 with 16GB and 256GB, about £400, and £1,000 for a tablet at about £500, such as a Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE at £509: these run local models, and the website can be built on the device itself. The German-made Volla tablet with the de-Googled /e/OS is a European alternative. The Pi is the cheaper way in at each level; what is left of each pledge after the hardware pays for the setup, the site, the team inside it, support, shipping and the platform's fees. The UK is the base goal; Portugal is the first stretch goal; backers vote on the countries after it, and on iOS. All-or-nothing: if we do not reach the goal, nobody pays and we build nothing. And we launch on our own, with Android and open source, and talk to device makers once it works.

item.title: What is a sovereign website: defining the category the way serverless was defined, a website you own and can move, built only on commodity technology because one proprietary part anywhere in the middle is enough to lock you in, seven principles, a sovereignty maturity model from rented to proven, and the proof that the same site runs on every host, in Europe and on your own computer
item.description: I searched for "sovereign website" and found almost nothing. That is an opportunity: we get to define the category, the way serverless was defined, with principles anyone can test a site against. A sovereign website is a website you own and can move. Moving is the hard part, and the lesson I do not think has been learned is that one proprietary component in the middle, however small, is enough to stop you: nobody can move the site for you without rebuilding that part, so you cannot even pay your way out. Lock-in comes from the domain, the technology and the platform alike. So a sovereign website is built only on commodity technology, its content and schema in open formats, its domain in its owner's name. This piece proposes seven principles, a maturity model from level 0, rented, to level 5, sovereign and proven, and a proof every Sovereign Agentic Website should carry: the same commit deployed by one pipeline to GitHub Pages, Cloudflare, Netlify, Azure, AWS, a European host and your own computer. Agentic is how we build them; sovereign is what they are. The principles belong at sovereignwebsite.org.

item.title: Sovereign websites, the investment case: PrompTugal's investor decks rewritten for a deliverable that is needed everywhere, in every language, in a market built on rent and lock-in, a one-off delivery that is already fully agentic, value given before payment through a demo in a vault, a long list of upsells, and why this is now a proper, scalable, investable architecture
item.description: The investor decks we made for PrompTugal are good, and the structure carries over almost slide for slide. What changes is the product, and this one I think is investable in a way a newsroom is not. A Sovereign Agentic Website is one deliverable that every small business in the world needs, that works in any language and culture, and that walks into a market that is large, inefficient and built on rent and lock-in. The first sale is small and complete: one payment for a site that is the owner's, with CI, tests, security checks, five designs and a team of five to seven agents already inside it, more than almost anyone has today, so we under-promise and over-deliver. The value comes first, because the demo is their own website, in five versions, sealed in a vault before they pay. The cost to serve is low, with no servers of ours and the team running on the owner's own AI. And there is a long list of upsells on a site they already own: their domain, more languages, a shop without a backend, the full team, moving from Wix or WordPress, other cells. The code is open; the velocity, and the years of learning underneath, are the moat. Now the question is go to market.

item.title: Simple on top of years: why a startup has to find something very easy, very narrow and able to scale, why building from the bottom up, from provenance, understanding and determinism, ended in a simple product anyway, and how a website in five designs opened from a QR code sits on a CI pipeline, zero-knowledge sharing, sgit, vaults, keys and agentic teams, each learnt on its own
item.description: My view of startups has always been that you have to find something very easy: a narrow use case, at scale, that somebody can just use. What is odd is how I got to one. For the last couple of years I have been building from the bottom up, starting from provenance, from understanding and from determinism, because I do not want the black magic. You would expect that to end in something complicated. It ended in something simple: a person scans a QR code and sees their own website in five designs, and if they say yes it becomes theirs, with a team of agents inside it. That simple thing sits on layers I learnt one at a time, each for its own reason: a CI pipeline and tests on every change, almost the first thing I built; a file-sharing service where the server never holds the key, which taught me pricing and payments and also that "the technology worked, the use case was not there yet"; sgit, Git's model encrypted; vaults a web page can open; keys and secrets as QR codes; agentic teams with briefs and behaviour policies; and a factory that turns one commit into a site. None was built for this. Connecting them is the product, and the learning is the moat.

item.title: Your website, from a vault: how to show someone five versions of their own website without publishing anything, sealed in an encrypted sgit vault and opened with a QR code, a link or a zip on one drop page, the demo pipeline from a name to an email, and how a demo becomes their sovereign website without starting again
item.description: There are a lot of people I want to show a Sovereign Agentic Website to, and the best way is to show them their own: five versions of it, made by agents. The problem is that a demo cannot be public. Our repositories and sites are public by default, and "public but not linked" has never felt right. The answer has been in front of us: encrypted vaults. The demo cell takes a name, researches only public information, builds five designs, has them reviewed, and seals all five into one sgit vault. The person gets a QR code, a link with the key after the #, or a zip, and drops it on one page, which decrypts the vault in their browser and shows their site in a sandboxed frame, with a banner and the five designs one tap apart. Nothing is published, the key never reaches a server, and if they say yes, the factory makes their repository from the same vault, so the demo becomes the first chapter of their site's history. This piece maps the workflow and the pipeline, and what is still to build.

item.title: A website with a team inside: why a Sovereign Agentic Website is delivered not as a site but as a site with six or seven agents already set up and coordinated in its repository, a conductor, a designer, a writer, a developer, a reviewer, a translator and a keeper, each with a role and a behaviour policy, and what that means for the person who owns it
item.description: We are not just delivering a website. What a Sovereign Agentic Website hands over is a site with a team inside it: six or seven agents already set up in its repository and already coordinated. A conductor the owner talks to in plain words, who turns a request into a plan and hands out the work; a designer, a writer and a developer who make the change; a reviewer who checks the claims, prices, privacy and security before the owner sees anything; a translator for every language the site is in; and a keeper for the weekly care, broken links, speed, accessibility and the domain's renewal. Each has a brief and a behaviour policy in the repository, every change is a signed commit, and nothing goes live until the owner says yes. A florist who asks for a Mother's Day page by Friday does not get a tool to learn; she gets a team that does it. And because the team lives in her repository, it is hers too: when the site moves, the team moves with it.

item.title: Designing sovereignwebsite.ai: the brief for the team that will build the site of our first mass-market product, how the stack now has four layers, SGit, RiskMandate, AgentiCCells and Sovereign Website, six ways to say what it is, the ten pages, the sovereignty maturity model at its centre, how to build the site as a sovereign website itself, and five homepage designs to choose from
item.description: Sovereign Website is our first mass-market product, and its site, sovereignwebsite.ai, is next. This is the brief for the team that builds it, written in public so that the agents and the people can work from the same page. It starts with how everything we have talked about now stacks up: SGit for encrypted, versioned vaults; RiskMandate for the behaviour policies that bound what agents do; AgentiCCells for agentic teams; and on top, Sovereign Website, the first layer a small business can buy without knowing the others exist. Then six ways to say what it is, from "Built by agents, owned by you" to "Where is your website, from 0 to 5?". Then the ten pages of the first version, with a sovereignty maturity model from level 0, rented, to level 5, sovereign and proven, at the centre, and a one-minute self-check. Then how to build the site: as a sovereign website itself, in the SovereignWebsite organisation, five designs by a design agent, every claim on it true of the site. And five homepage designs, as every site we make starts with five.
